Wording and code match the cell (page 35, number 2, grade 5 column: one sentence, nothing else in the cell, no boldface). An example turned into a limit: the official sentence introduces the three ways in which information may be presented with a word meaning that they are among the media and formats, so others are not excluded. The Summary gives the three in a parenthesis as what the media and formats are, with no word marking them as included examples, and Limits repeats them as the forms the information takes. Limits also states that the source is not read silently by the child; the official text does not say that (information presented in a visual or quantitative format can be something the child reads). Mark the three as included among diverse media and formats, and drop the limit about silent reading or present it as the pack's inference.

Round 2, after the fix. Read in number 2 of the grade 5 column on PDF page 35 (page image, also at 300 dpi): one sentence, nothing else in the cell, no boldface. Code equal. The fix resolved both points of round 1: the Summary and Limits now give the three ways of presenting as included among the media and formats, with others not excluded, and Limits no longer says anything about silent reading. Noted, not counted: the Summary says the text is read aloud to the child, where the statement does not say to whom it is read; no condition changes.

Compared by eye in number 3 of the grade 5 column, Speaking and Listening table, PDF page 35 (also at 330 dpi, and letter by letter against the text layer of that cell). Two words differ; everything else is equal, including the closing California mark, and nothing else stands in the cell. (1) The eighteenth word: the record has the noun in the singular, the PDF prints it in the plural (one more letter at its end). (2) The twenty-fifth word: the record repeats the three-letter joining word that also stands two words earlier, which leaves the final clause ungrammatical; the PDF prints a three-letter determiner there (the two differ in their last letter), so that the final clause covers whatever fallacies there are. The PDF reading is the grammatical one in both places, so the export row has two typing errors, which the importer copied faithfully. The Summary already follows the PDF reading in both places. California addition, as the PDF boldface shows it: the sixth to eighth words (the joining word and the second kind of source) and, after the comma, the whole final clause from the twenty-first word to the end, with the mark; the rest is plain. The flag (true) is right. For the fixer: Limits can say which parts are California's as the adopted PDF shows them, and that the PDF differs from the stored wording in two words. The record's wording itself can only be right when the importer may correct the export from the PDF.

Round 2. The wording is now right: it is the export's as corrected from the adopted document at two places, both export typing errors (the eighteenth word, a noun given back its plural ending; the twenty-fifth word, a three-letter joining word replaced by the three-letter determiner the document prints). It equals number 3 of the grade 5 column on PDF page 35 word for word (page image, also at 300 dpi), with the closing California mark; nothing else stands in the cell. Both corrections are right, and the round 1 reason (wording-differs) is resolved. Boldface on the page: the sixth to eighth words and, after the comma, the final clause with the mark. Code equal. The Summary is faithful to the corrected wording, and nothing in the Summary or the Design notes follows the export's two defects. One fault stands in Limits, first sentence: after naming the two kinds of source it adds that the source is not a printed text. The statement names a speaker or a media source and excludes nothing; printed media fall inside the general term it uses, so this is a limit the official text does not state, and a designer would rely on it. For the fixer: end that sentence after the two kinds of source (or say that the statement does not say which media are meant). The rest of Limits is right.

Round 3. The round 2 reason is resolved: the first Limits sentence now ends after the two kinds of source and no longer excludes printed text. One new sentence says that the wording is the export's as corrected from the adopted document at two places. That is what the importer's list holds for this code (two corrections, both export typing errors: a noun given back its plural ending, and a joining word replaced by the determiner the document prints), and both are right on the page image (PDF page 35, grade 5 column, number 3). The wording equals the cell word for word, with the closing California mark; nothing else stands in the cell. Code equal. Read whole: Summary faithful (summarising what either kind of source puts forward; how each claim is backed; finding fallacies of logic and analysing them) and in the pack's own shape (two sentences; the middle part recast, the last part reordered). Limits right: the two kinds of source, every claim linked to its support, no fallacies named, and the mark that does not show which words are California's (boldface on the page: the sixth to eighth words and the final clause with the mark).

Wording and code match the cell (page 29, number 2, grade 5 column: opening line and parts a to e in order, nothing else in the cell, no boldface). A changed condition in the Summary's last sentence: part e asks only that the concluding statement or section have to do with the information or explanation presented; the Summary says it "follows from" it. That is a stronger relation, the one the narrative standard of this grade sets for its conclusion (W.5.3, part e); for this statement the official relation is the looser one, the same as in the opinion standard (W.5.1, part d), where the Summary has it right. Change the last sentence to say that the closing relates to what was presented. The rest of the Summary and the Design notes are faithful; Limits keeps formatting, illustrations and multimedia apart.
